connection_sequence.description:
BG-BT1X (1-probe): Connect → discover services → enable notify on ff01, ff03, ff05, 2a19 → write fea1b2c3e40000 to ff02 (handshake) → read ff01 for temperatures.
BBQ-4BW (4-probe): Connect → discover services → enable notify on ff01, ff03, ff04, ff05, ff06 → write fb000000000000 to ff02 → receive 12-char challenge on ff03 → calculate verify response (full algorithm under the verify_response command; source: the app's BBQ-4BW helper) → write fcXXXXXXXXXXXX to ff02 → read ff04 (status) → read ff01 (temps) → read 2a19 (battery) → query all settings (target temp per probe, unit, display time, compensation, sound, firmware, alarm, wifi, light, probe color).
Timing: the app waits ~500 ms after connect before the first write, and chains subsequent init commands with ~120 ms handler delays; auto-connect triggers only when RSSI > -85 dBm. IBT-4WB differs: its fb challenge arrives on ff02 and the verify frame is 16 chars — see the DIALECT WARNING in device.notes.

device.name: Inkbird BBQ Thermometer (BLE)
device.notes:
Covers Inkbird BLE BBQ thermometers using direct BLE protocol: IBT-2X (BG-BT1X, 1 probe), IBT-4XS (4 probes), IBT-6X (6 probes), IBBQ-4BW (4 probes + WiFi via Tuya), and related models.
Protocol reverse-engineered by static analysis of the official Inkbird Android app — specifically its per-model device handlers for the BBQ-4BW and BG-BT1X families.
The app uses two BLE stacks: direct BLE (InkBluetoothManager) for BBQ thermometers, and Tuya/Thing Smart BLE SDK for newer devices. This spec documents the direct BLE protocol.
All protocol UUIDs use template 0000ffXX-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. Service is 0000ff00. Temperature data is little-endian signed 16-bit integers raw in device units; the unit (°F or °C) must be queried separately via command 04.
Error values: 0x7ffe, 0x7fff, 0x8000 indicate probe disconnected/fault.
Newer firmware advertises different local names: a real 2025-era IBT-2X-B advertises "Inkbird@IBT-2X-B" (ble_monitor issue #1443), which none of the classic prefixes match — "Inkbird@" is included in the prefix lists.
Connection requires a handshake: BG-BT1X uses fixed code fea1b2c3e40000 (an alternate fixed frame fea1b2c3e4f5f5 is written by the config activity); BBQ-4BW, IBT-4XS, IBT-26S and the 2-probe IBT-2XB use challenge-response (fb000000000000 to ff02, challenge on ff03 with fb prefix, fc+12-hex response back to ff02). The BBQ-4BW verify-code algorithm is fully recovered and given in full under the verify_response command below: deterministic sqrt/mod/pow math on the 6-byte challenge (no timestamp, no CRC), read out of the app's BBQ-4BW helper.
CAVEAT — two incompatible BLE protocol families ship under the same model names: IBT-2X / IBT-4XS also exist on the older 0xfff0 "iBBQ/EasyBBQ" binary protocol (chars fff1-fff5, fixed-credentials login, s16le temps in 0.1 °C — uucidl ibbq-thermometer-protocol gist, gleeds/cloudbbq; covered by the sibling spec ibbq-meat-thermo, app com.inkbird.ibbtgo). Discovery must key on the advertised service UUID (ff00 vs fff0), not the name.
The ASCII-hex 14-char framing documented here is specific to the BBQ line. The INT-12-BW / INT-14-BW variant uses binary <LEN><TYPE>[PAYLOAD] framing on ff02 with temps in 0.1 °C and a different auth (01 fb challenge → response = LE16 ms + LE32 unix time + two-stage CRC-8) — recovered by paul43210/inkbird-bw-ble (17 captured test vectors in auth/python/auth.py).
DIALECT WARNING — IBT-4WB: this 4-probe model matches this spec's discovery keys (IBT- name prefix, ff00 service) but speaks a different dialect of the protocol; a client written strictly to this spec would connect and then misparse it (per the app's IBT-4WB handler and model): - Auth is timestamp+CRC based: the fb challenge arrives on ff02 (not
  ff03), and the response mixes the challenge with the client's current
  unix-ms clock — LE16 of the ms-within-second, LE32 of the seconds,
  then CRC-8/DVB-S2 over those 6 bytes; CRC-8/CDMA2000 over the
  challenge is computed but not sent.
- The verify frame breaks the universal 14-char rule: the app writes
  "fc" + 14 hex chars (8 bytes, 16 chars total) to ff02.
- Device status is parsed from ff03 (not ff04) with its own bitfield:
  charging at bit 32, WiFi status at bits 33-37.
- ff01 temps are 8 hex chars (s32 LE) per probe, not 4; the fault
  sentinels are 32-bit (7ffffffe, 7fffffff, 80000001), and byte 16
  (chars 32-33) carries the device ambient temp in °C.
IBT-4RT also exists in the app's model list (4 probes); it is treated as protocol-compatible with this spec but has no documented model-specific code path — listed as compatible-but-undocumented.
Timing and scan behavior (BBQ-4BW, from the app's handler delays): ~500 ms settle after connect before the handshake write, ~120 ms delays between chained init commands, and an auto-connect RSSI threshold of > -85 dBm (from its BBQ-4BW handler chain).
Encoding nuance: the uniform s16le rule below is what the multi-probe models use (shortValue()); the 1-probe BG-BT1X instead parses ff01 as UNSIGNED u16 and treats only 7fff/8000 as fault on that path.
No BLE pairing/bonding required; all commands work over unencrypted BLE GATT.
Schema gaps (device-specs/schema.json not modified): no dedicated field for byte-order notation, signed vs unsigned field typing, multi-byte reverse-endian bitfields, or challenge-response auth flows. These are documented in notes and field annotations.

credentials.notes: No WiFi passphrase crosses the BLE link documented here. The handshake codes are fixed constants shared by every unit of a model, not secrets: all commands run over unencrypted GATT, readable by anyone in range. WiFi provisioning on the IBBQ-4BW goes through the Tuya SDK, which this spec does not document.

factory_reset.description:
`false` rather than `unknown`: Inkbird's own documentation covers pairing, charging and use, and describes no reset control on any of these units; the sealed lithium battery on the IBT-4XS means there is not even a battery to pull.
What people reach for a reset to fix is almost always the exclusivity problem instead, and Inkbird are explicit about it: one phone talks to one unit at a time, and a phone that has been paired with a different Inkbird thermometer has to have that record deleted before it will connect to this one. That is recorded in `pairing.exclusivity`, and it is the actual fix.
factory_reset.effect: No factory reset, and nothing on the device that one would clear. The thermometer holds no credentials and no bond — it takes a connection from any central with no pairing code at all — and its alarm and unit settings are pushed from the app each session rather than persisted as state a user would need to wipe.

methods.description: Scan for the Inkbird device by name prefix, connect, and read GATT characteristics directly. Optional handshake varies by model.

steps.action: Power the thermometer on so it begins advertising.
Scan for the Inkbird name prefix and connect to service 0000ff00.
Perform the model's handshake: BG-BT1X takes the fixed code fea1b2c3e40000; IBBQ-4BW uses challenge-response with a verify-code calculation.
Query the unit with command 04 before decoding — temperatures are raw little-endian signed 16-bit device units, and the same number means °F or °C depending on this setting.
steps.expect: Temperature readings. 0x7ffe, 0x7fff and 0x8000 mean the probe is disconnected or faulty, not a real temperature.

setup.notes: No provisioning, pairing, or account required for BLE-only operation. Simply scan, connect, optionally perform the handshake, and read temperature data. WiFi-enabled variants (IBBQ-4BW) also work over BLE without WiFi setup.

rejoin.notes: No bond is held: any client may reconnect and repeat the handshake once the previous one disconnects. For the IBBQ-4BW, this covers BLE only — its WiFi credentials are managed by the Tuya stack.

variants.notes: Basic BLE-only single-probe thermometer. Parses ff01 as UNSIGNED u16 (not the s16le of the multi-probe models); fault sentinels on this path are 7fff/8000 only.
Two-probe variant under IBT-2XB name. Uses the same fb000000000000 challenge-response handshake as the 4-probe models.

6-probe thermometer. ff01 extends as documented, but the ff04 status bitfield differs from the 4-probe layout: single combined fault bit per probe at bits 6-11, WiFi status at bits 36-41 — see the ff04 notes.
6-probe thermometer. Same protocol family presumed; no model-specific code path in the app (protocol unverified).

variants.handshake: challenge-response, timestamp+CRC variant (fb on ff02, 16-char fc verify frame)
variants.notes: DIFFERENT DIALECT — matches this spec's discovery keys but is not wire-compatible: timestamp+CRC8 auth on ff02, status on ff03 with its own bitfield, 8-hex-char (s32 LE) per-probe ff01 temps with 32-bit sentinels. See the DIALECT WARNING in device.notes.
Listed in the app's model constants (TYPE_IBT_4RT); presumed compatible with this spec but undocumented — no model-specific parser was found.

characteristics.description: Multi-probe temperature data. Little-endian signed 16-bit integers per probe plus ambient.
characteristics.name: temperature_data
characteristics.notes: For 1-probe devices (BG-BT1X), only bytes 0-1 are valid. For 4-probe devices, bytes 0-9 (5 × int16: 4 probes + ambient). For 6-probe devices, bytes 0-13 (7 × int16: 6 probes + ambient). Error values: 0x7ffe, 0x7fff, 0x8000 indicate probe disconnected or fault. Raw values are in the device's configured temperature unit.

commands.description:
Calculated verify response (12 hex chars after fc). Fully recovered algorithm (from the app's BBQ-4BW helper, getBleGetVerifyCode) — deterministic math on the 12-char challenge C, no timestamp, no CRC:

  v1 = int(C[2:4]  + C[0:2],  16)   # LE u16 of challenge bytes 0-1
  v2 = int(C[6:8]  + C[4:6],  16)   # LE u16 of bytes 2-3
  v3 = int(C[10:12]+ C[8:10], 16)   # LE u16 of bytes 4-5
  s  = int(sqrt(v1) - 1) if v1 odd else int(sqrt(v1) - 3)
  r  = (v2 % s) if (v2 != 0 and s != 0) else 0
  q  = int(sqrt(v2))
  t  = ((v3 % 255) + r + q + int(C[10:12], 16)) // 4   # integer division
  response = hex2(s) + hex2(r) + hex2((r % 16) + (s % 238))
           + hex2(q) + hex2((v1 % 15) ** 2) + hex2(t)

where hex2(x) is StringUtils.intToHex2(x, 2): lowercase hex digits left-padded with zeros to 2 chars (pad-only, no truncation or masking). A value above 0xff would emit more than 2 chars, but none can occur — every term is provably <= 0xff: s <= 254 (int(sqrt) of a u16 is <= 255), r < s so r <= 253, (r % 16) + (s % 238) <= 15 + 237 = 252, q <= 255, (v1 % 15)**2 <= 196, and t <= (254+253+255+255)//4 = 254. The response is therefore always exactly 12 hex chars and the frame "fc" + response always 14 chars. (Degenerate edge: an even v1 of 0, 2 or 4 makes s negative, which would crash the app's hex2 digit loop with a negative array index — real challenges do not hit it.) If C is not 12 chars the app returns it unchanged.

response_types.description: Verify challenge (12 hex chars). Triggers verify response calculation.
Device status acknowledgment. Client should re-read ff04 after receiving this.

Target temp response (probe-specific). Payload: 2-char bitmask, 2-char mode, 4-char high temp LE, 4-char low temp LE. Mode byte: 01 = low threshold only, 10 = high threshold only, 11 = both, per the app's BBQ-4BW model.
Target temp response (alternate probe mask). Same payload format as 01, mode bytes identical.
Temp unit response. Payload byte 0: 0x46 = °F, else °C.
Temp unit response (alternate). Same as 03.
Display time response. Payload bytes 0-1 LE = seconds.
Display time response (alternate). Same as 07.
Temp compensation response. Per-probe signed byte offsets.
Temp compensation response (alternate). Same as 09.
Sound switch response. Payload: 0x11 = on, 0x5a = off.
Sound switch response (alternate). Same as 0b.
Firmware version response. Payload is ASCII hex.
Alarm mode response. Byte 0: 0x01=interval, 0x11=times; Byte 1: ring count.
Alarm mode response (alternate). Same as 10.
WiFi switch response. 0x01=on, 0x00=off.
WiFi switch response (alternate). Same as 12.
Light switch response. 0x01=on, 0x00=off.
Probe color response. 8 hex chars, 2 per probe.
Device power-off notification.

bitfield.description: WiFi connection status for dual-mode devices (4-probe layout; IBT-26S uses bits 36-41 instead).
bitfield.name: wifi_status

data_format.notes:
The raw hex string must be byte-reversed before bit interpretation. Example: raw "a1b2c3" → reversed bytes "c3b2a1" → interpret bits of resulting integer.
SCOPE: this layout is 4-probe-specific — it is exactly what Bbq4bwItemModel.bleParseDeviceStatus parses, so it applies to the IBBQ-4BW / BBQ-4BW / IBT-4XS / IBT-24S family only. The IBT-26S uses a different, wider layout (parsed as a long in the app's IBT-26S model): probe alert bits 0-5 (probeNum-1), a SINGLE combined fault bit per probe at bits 6-11 (probeNum+5) instead of the 4-probe high/low/sensor triple at bits 4-15, and WiFi status at bits 36-41. Do not apply the bitfield below to a 6-probe unit.
CAVEAT: bits 16-19 below (ambient alarms, charging, backlight) were stated in earlier revisions of this spec but are UNEVIDENCED — the app parses only bits 0-15 and the WiFi bits 20-25; no parser for bits 16-19 exists anywhere in it. Treat them as unverified guesses, not protocol fact.
